extracted.intended_audience: labor-law practitioners, NLRB adjudicators, employers, unions, and counsel addressing joint-employer questions under the NLRA
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factors for determining whether an entity is a joint employer under the National Labor Relations Act, applying common-law agency principles (focus on the right to control, reserved/indirect control, and which matters bear on essential terms and conditions of employment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to control (not its exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinative factor is an entity's right to control the manner and means of performance, rather than the actual exercise of that control — 'it is the right to control, not the actual exercise of control that is significant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations and authority repeated throughout: courts and Restatements emphasize the 'right to control' as the vital test; actual exercise of control is unnecessary to establish an employment relationship. Use evidence of reserved or potential authority over manner/means as probative even if not exercised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary company-to-company contract terms are immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary contract terms providing generally for engaging workers and setting general price terms do not constitute an exercise of direct control over essential terms and conditions of employment and therefore are not relevant to joint-employer analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion warns that if simple contract provisions for engaging workers or setting price automatically created joint-employer status, the standard would be unworkable; such routine contractual allocations between companies should be excluded from the joint-employer inquiry unless they bear on essential employment terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved (contractual) right of control can be dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity's contractual reservation of authority (a reserved right to control) over the manner of performance may render it a common-law employer or joint employer even if that authority was never exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases hold that explicit agreements about control can be dispositive; courts have found employer status based solely on reserved rights (e.g., contractual delegation or retained supervisory authority). Look to the parties' written agreements for explicit reservation-of-control clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control (through intermediaries) is probative, not 'direct' control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control exercised through an intermediary is mediated (indirect) rather than direct, but such indirect control can be weighed and may be independently probative of joint-employer status in appropriate factual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treats intermediary-mediated control as indirect control and instructs that it may be considered, especially where the intermediary merely ferries orders from the putative joint employer to workers. Examples include authority exercised through supervisors of a contractor or through regulatory-authority-derived powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control must bear on essential terms and conditions of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Only control that bears on the employees' essential terms and conditions of employment is relevant to establishing a joint-employer relationship; control over routine components of a company-to-company contract is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board and courts must focus on whether reserved or exercised control concerns core employment terms (hiring, firing, supervision, discipline, compensation, benefits, hours, work rules), rather than peripheral commercial contract terms. The Final Rule incorporates this distinction (see Sec. 103.40(f) referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant control standard (two-entity comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint-employer relationship exists when two entities 'exercise significant control over the same employees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have phrased the joint-employer test around whether both entities exercise significant control; consider the extent and practical effect of each entity's authority in parallel when two principals may share control over workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated control factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant indicia include the right to hire and fire, the right to supervise, ability to promulgate work rules and assignments, set conditions of employment (compensation, benefits, hours), training, promotion, discipline, and setting work schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific factors (quoted and aggregated from cases like Knitter, Bristol, Plaso, Graves, Perry) are repeatedly used by courts as central evidence of control. Evaluators should check for direct or reserved authority over each of these domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who, when, and how (agent-specific and temporal aspects of control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond establishing that control exists, the joint-employer inquiry asks who is exercising that control, when the control is exercised, and how it is exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes parsing which entity acted (or could act), the timing and context of control, and the mechanisms (direct supervision, written policies, contractual vetoes, intermediated instructions) — important for attributing control in multi-entity relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total factual-context assessment under common-law agency principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments should be based on the total factual context and judged in light of pertinent common-law agency principles rather than applying a single mechanically decisive factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite NLRB v. United Ins. Co. and other authority for the totality-of-circumstances approach; adjudicators should synthesize evidence across multiple indicia rather than rely on isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to take corrective measures under reserved control may give rise to liability
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity that contractually reserved a right to control but never exercised it could nevertheless be liable (e.g., for discriminatory acts) if it failed to prevent or correct unlawful conduct within its reserved authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitaker and related authorities suggest that reserved vetoes or disciplinary authorities, even if never used, can create an obligation to act and potential liability if the entity does not use its reserved authority to prevent or remedy unlawful behavior; this supports treating reserved control as potentially operative for remedies.
